Garran Hill · Then & Now

One century between the photographs. The gate remains.

Then
The Estate · Pinehurst, NC

Some houses hold history. This one shaped it.

The gates have opened onto the same circular drive since 1916. The house at the end of it has not moved.

Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918

He named it Garran Hill. He never spent a night here.

Born in Cary, North Carolina. Co-founder of Doubleday, Page & Company. Editor of The Atlantic Monthly. Ambassador to the Court of St. James, 1913 to 1918 — the years the world came apart and he worked from London to hold the alliance together. He bought one thousand acres in Moore County in February 1913 and began building. His son Ralph supervised. Leonard Tufts sent the craftsmen. Page returned from London in December 1918. He died ten days later.

He sailed for London. Construction was supervised by his son Ralph Page, from Boston architectural plans, with builders from Leonard Tufts’ Pinehurst building world.

He wrote home about one thing.

“Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game.”

Walter Hines Page — Letter to Ralph Page, 1918

Co-founder of Doubleday, Page & Co. Editor of The Atlantic Monthly. A plaque in Westminster Abbey. Garran Hill was built for a life Page never had the chance to live.

“The farm — the farm — the farm.”

Walter Hines Page · From His Letters · 1913–1918

“The farm — the farm — the farm.”

Neo-Georgian · 1915–1916

Pinehurst hands. A century of brick and proportion.

Leonard Tufts sent his craftsmen. The brickwork, the arched fanlights, the herringbone entry floor — all of it built by hand, in Moore County, between 1915 and 1916. Thomas O'Shea's 1999–2001 restoration honored every decision they made. What you see today is what Walter Hines Page commissioned. Nothing has been softened. Nothing has been updated for its own sake.

Boston plans. Pinehurst hands. Garran Hill in brick, 1916.

The Threshold · 1916

The door has been open since 1916.

The brick reads Garran Hill 1916 in the stone beneath your feet. Through the open door: herringbone brick, warm light, the volute staircase turning to the right. Everything you are about to see was here before you arrived — and will be here long after.

Restoration
The Restoration · 1999–2001

What was original stayed original.

The approach was disciplined: nothing replaced that could be restored, nothing added that the original design didn't call for. The shell cabinets in the dining room are original. The herringbone brick in the foyer is original. The mahogany volute staircase has turned the same curve since 1916.

Matching the old brick on the portico alone took three months. That is the standard to which every decision in this restoration was held.

Thirty-six drawings — elevations, floor plans, foundation, framing, portico, kitchen, primary suite, library built-ins, trim profiles. Every decision documented before a board came down. The drawings transfer with the property.

A preservation easement carries a North Carolina tax credit of 25% of fair market value, up to $500,000.

In 1916, those were saplings.

Now they are a forest.

1916 — The day they were planted

Today — One hundred and nine years later

The Foyer · Entry Procession

The arched fanlights. The herringbone brick underfoot.

The mahogany volute staircase rises to the right. The leaded glass is original. The brick pattern beneath your feet was laid in 1916. This is the first thing the house shows you — and it doesn’t apologize for any of it.

The Interior

Six principal rooms. Each one a different answer.

Enter the House  →
The Salon

The house's great living room.

Nearly forty feet from end to end. The red walls pull everything inward and warm. The eye goes to the white Georgian fireplace first — carved mantel, art arranged above it with intention. Then to the far end, where glass doors open to the brick terrace. Two seating areas. Arched fanlights. The Salon is the room where everyone eventually lands.

The Drawing Room · The Blue Room

Tiled fireplace. Intimate scale. A spiral stair to the office above.

The fire is lit in the frame and the whole room shifts register — from formal to private. Blue walls, white woodwork, Delft-tiled fireplace surround. The Drawing Room is smaller than the Salon by design: it was always meant to be the room you retreat to. The bookshelves flank it. The flame holds the center.

"Blue-and-white tile, firelight, and a spiral stair — the Drawing Room keeps its own rhythm."

The Dining Room

The table has been set in this room since 1916.

The dining table anchors the room — long, dark, centered under the chandelier. The shell cabinets flanking the fireplace are original to the house. The wallpaper is a print that has been here since the restoration and reads like the room always knew what it wanted to be. The folding screen that divides the room from the hall folds and disappears. It has been doing that since 1916.

The Library

Three walls. Floor to ceiling. The ladder is still there.

Natural light comes in through tall windows, softened into the kind that makes an afternoon feel like permission. The shelves go to the ceiling on three walls, lined with books. The rolling ladder is there — functional, not decorative. Walter Hines Page was an editor and publisher. He co-founded Doubleday, Page & Company. He edited The Atlantic Monthly. He would have walked into this room and felt immediately at home.

When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

Kitchen & Butler’s Pantry

White cabinetry. Dark granite. Island. Four windows. Room to cook.

The island is black against white cabinetry. Heart-pine floors run beneath it — original to the 1999–2001 restoration. Four windows face the grounds and let the morning light in. The wallpaper is a black-and-white print that carries the history without announcing it. Two farm sinks. The kitchen is serious about cooking, and the grounds are visible through every window.

The adjoining side porch carries hot and cold water, built-in cabinets and shelves — full potting and grounds support. The kitchen runs the full service life of the house.

Sheet 12 of the restoration drawings documents the kitchen cabinetry in elevation — cooking wall, cornice, pantry, desk, TV cabinet, and potting side-porch work all drawn before they were built.

The Social Rooms

The Salon — The house’s great living room, long and gracious, arranged in two seating areas with glass doors opening to the brick terrace.

The Dining Room — Original frontispiece. 17 × 19 ft. Disappearing folding screen still works.

The Drawing Room — The Blue Room. Blue-and-white tiled fireplace, intimate scale. A spiral stair rises to the second-floor office above.

The Library · Details

The books have been here longer than anyone alive.

The shelving on three walls holds what was left behind and what was brought in. The rolling ladder runs the full width. The French doors open to the grounds. In the afternoon, the light through those doors crosses the floor and reaches the spines on the opposite wall. This is the room the house was built around.

When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

The Primary Suite

A fireplace. Two windows. The grounds on both sides.

The fireplace is centered, flanked by two upholstered armchairs. Soft natural light from the windows to the left. The palette is pastel — yellows, greens, a touch of blue — quiet colors for a room designed to be a place of actual rest. The primary suite occupies the corner of the second floor. Mornings here face the trees.

The primary balcony — 24 × 11 ft — faces the grounds.

The Staircase · 1916

The same curve since 1916.

The mahogany volute turns from the foyer in a single continuous arc — black railing, wooden treads, the wallpaper rising beside it. It has not been replaced. It has not been rebuilt. It has been climbed every day, by every person who has lived in this house, since the craftsmen Leonard Tufts sent finished it in 1916. The curve is the original curve.

The stair still gives the entry its first gesture of grace.

Private Rooms

Primary Suite. Balcony. Four bedrooms.

The primary suite has a fireplace, custom wall panels, and a 24 × 11 ft balcony overlooking the grounds. Four bedrooms total — each shaped during restoration for proportion and light.

Primary bath, primary closet, and upper hall all documented in the restoration drawings. The private floor was treated with the same architectural discipline as the social rooms below.

Primary Bath · The Jewel Box

Mirror. Marble. Ornament that earns its place.

The primary bath reads like a jewel box — the wallpaper is floral and dense, the sink is centered and ornate, the light is warm and deliberate. Everything in this room was chosen to contrast with the scale of the house around it. It is small on purpose. The detail is the point.

The Powder Room

Fuchsia chinoiserie. A room that does not apologize.

The fuchsia wallpaper is the whole point. Chinoiserie pattern, floor to ceiling, Tennessee marble beneath it. This is the most opinionated room in the house — designed to stop you, make you look, make you feel something. It works. It has always worked.

The House Keeps Secrets

Garran Hill rewards the close observer.

The curved banister. The original hardware. The way the light moves through the leaded glass at different hours. This house was built by craftsmen who cared about things no one would ever notice — and then noticed them anyway. The secrets are still here. They reveal themselves slowly.

The house still knows how to keep a secret.

The Grounds · A Private History · 1959–1984

Horses. Hounds. Peacocks. Native hollies on every path.

Betty Dumaine kept this land for twenty-five years. She brought horses to the grounds of Garran Hill — thoroughbreds, hunters, a life organized around animals and land and the particular pleasure of a place that required real attention. One horse she buried here. Blue Fox. The stone is still standing in the shade of the trees she planted. The iron post beside the drive still carries the ring. Someone still puts flowers at the grave.

Betty Dumaine’s Hollycrest years carried horses, hounds, peacocks, native hollies, and old Pinehurst lore to the estate. Her Irish hunter, Blue Fox, is buried on the grounds. Someone still puts flowers there.

Someone still puts flowers there.

The Grounds
The Terrace · Open Air

The world outside these gates does not exist here.

The terrace opens off the Salon through glass doors. Brick underfoot — the same material as the house, the same that engraves 1916 at the threshold. The lattice railing is white. The loungers face outward toward the treeline. On a clear afternoon the sky above the canopy is an uninterrupted blue. This is where the house ends and the land begins.

Brick underfoot. French doors behind. Garden beyond.

The Pool · Salt Water · 2022

Twenty by forty feet. The gate opens onto it directly.

Through old iron gates, the 20×40 in-ground concrete pool catches afternoon light inside its brick walls. Converted from chlorine to saltwater in 2022, it belongs to the landscape rather than interrupting it.

The Wee Cottage · The Grounds

A cottage in the azaleas. Its own complete world.

Tucked into the grounds behind a wall of azaleas and tall trees, the Wee Cottage has its own entrance, its own scale, its own quality of light. Guest quarters. Studio. The possibility of a life lived slightly apart from the main house, on the same four-point-fifteen acres.

A small house within the larger story.

The Sporting Grounds

Tennis Ready for Renewal.

Two regulation tennis courts remain part of the estate’s sporting landscape, ready for renewal.

4.15 Acres · Moore County, North Carolina

From above, the estate explains itself.

Garran Hill sits within its own 4.15-acre circle — the surviving house core of a much larger Page-era farm.

Inside the gates: circular drive, lawn, brick terrace, pool, gardens, tennis, and shade.
